newsitem.title: JAPAN: OLYMPICS-NAGANO SAYS HIGHER DOWNILL SKI START ILLEGAL.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-NAGANO SAYS HIGHER DOWNILL SKI START ILLEGAL.

text.p: The wrangling over Nagano's Winter Olympics downhill skiing course took a fresh turn on Wednesday when the Games' chief organiser said it would be against the law to have a higher starting point.

"We have come to the stage where we have had to show legal reason why it cannot be raised," Makoto Kobayashi, director general of the Nagano Olympic Organising Committee (NAOC), told a news conference.

The bitter dispute with the International Ski Federation over the starting height has tarnished Nagano's image internationally, with the federation and even Japanese Olympic officials pushing Nagano to raise the start.
"The Environment Agency has said no to our requests to raise the start," Kobayashi said, "because doing so would break environmental laws by putting the start into a national park."
He said the government agency had given NAOC a document saying it would be illegal to raise the start and illegal to even put up temporary facilities in the national park.

The latest call to raise the start came from Japanese ski association chief Yoshiaki Tsutsumi, who said earlier this month that the start needed to be raised from 1,680 metres because the course was too short.
Kobayashi also said work was progressing on a computer system to distribute competition results for the February 7-22 Games and on ways to ease possible traffic jams.
About one-third of the 68 events next year are in or near the resort of Hakuba, 50 km west of Nagano on a windy, bottleneck of a highway.
The trip took more than 2-1/2 hours during a pre-Olympic ski jumping competition earlier this year.
"There were traffic problems during some pre-Olympic events but there were no traffic regulations in place then," Kobayashi said.
"We'll have extremely strict regulations in place during the Games," he said, with the goal of cutting regular traffic by 30 percent.
Kobayashi said work on the computer system to distribute results was "on track".
"I'm sure we'll have none of the problems that happened in Atlanta," he said, referring to the traffic chaos in the city last summer.
Kobayashi said NAOC was asking companies to help with promoting the Games and that Japan Airlines had agreed to show a promotional video on its international flights for the next three months.
He also said messages had been exchanged with North Korea about their participation in the Games but that no official application had been made yet.
More than 80 countries are expected to send about 3,000 athletes and officials to participate in the Games.
